newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan auto body says sharp export rise to fall off.
newsitem.headline: Japan auto body says sharp export rise to fall off.

text.p: A top Japanese auto official responded on Thursday to U.S. concerns about bilateral auto trade by saying that the jump in Japanese exports to the United States was unlikely to persist.

His comments came after U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky earlier this week said the U.S. automotive trade deficit with Japan was getting worse, and criticised Tokyo for falling short in fulfilling an agreement to open its market.
"I do not think exports will continue at the current speed," Takao Tominaga, vice chairman and executive managing director of the Japan Automobile Manufacturers' Association, told reporters in Tokyo.

"The sharp gain in exports was partly based on strong demand for sports-utility vehicles which are not produced by Japanese makers in the United States," Tominaga said, adding Japanese carmakers are expected to start making the vehicles in the United States in the future.
Japan exported 634,394 vehicles to the United States in the first half of 1997, up from 518,806 in the first six months of last year, but down from 724,947 in the 1995 period.
Japan's exports to the U.S. totalled 1.10 million vehicles for all of 1996, down 10.6 percent from 1.23 million in 1995.
Exports of U.S. cars to Japan in the January-June period of this fell 36.7 percent from a year earlier to 41,736 vehicles.
Tominaga said imports of U.S. cars had fallen off because Japan increased its consumption tax in April.
Tominaga also said that autos should not be singled out when discussing Japan-U.S. trade problems.
"Trade surplus issues should not be discussed by sector. The share of car exports in the total trade surplus is declining," Tominaga said.
He also said there was no need to introduce voluntary export restraints, which were in place from April 1981 until early 1994.
The restraints were replaced by a 1995 U.S.-Japan trade agreement, reached after bitter talks which took the two nations to the brink of a trade war.
The pact called on Tokyo to give foreign car and car parts suppliers more access and encourage more Japanese dealers to sell U.S. brand cars.
Both Barshefsky and Andrew Card, the president of the American Automobile Manufacturers' Association, have said there has not been enough progress on those points.
Barshefsky also said Japan had stalled on deregulating its car sector.
"That is of significant concern and inexcusable," Barshefsky said. "The number of vehicle dealerships is also not adequate."
Card's organisation has said that since the 1995 agreement was signed, 126 new dealerships had agreed to sell U.S. cars, far short of the 200 expected by the end of the first year.
"The 200 dealerships was the expectation of the U.S. manufacturers. It was not part of the agreement and not a commitment," Tominaga said.
Tominaga also said he does not want to see the dollar strengthening from the current level. The dollar was trading at about 118.25 yen on Thursday afternoon.
In mid-July, Card said an exchange rate of 95-105 yen to the dollar was an appropriate level.
